title: Pressure-cooker beetroot
subtitle: Tender, vibrant beetroot in 20 minutes
excerpt: Whole raw beetroot cooked under pressure until completely tender. No peeling before cooking, the skin slips off effortlessly after, leaving the full colour and flavour intact.
sourceNotes: Cooking beetroot whole in water or steam is the standard method across British and Eastern European cooking. The skin is removed after cooking, preserving the colour. The pressure-cooker method reduces the usual 45 to 60 minutes of boiling to about 20 minutes.

recipe.batchNotes: Cook a large batch and keep in the fridge for up to 5 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook and refrigerate whole, unpeeled, for up to 5 days. Peel and slice when needed.

content.text: Pressure-cooker beetroot is the fastest way to get from raw to tender beetroot with no effort. Whole, unpeeled beetroot go into the pot with a little water; 20 minutes at high pressure; then the skins slip off with a gentle rub under cold water. The flesh comes out vibrant, deeply coloured, and fully cooked.

Do not peel or cut the beetroot before cooking. The skin acts as a barrier that keeps the colour and sugars inside the vegetable during cooking. Peeled beetroot cooks unevenly and bleeds colour into the water, losing both flavour and pigment.
Wear rubber gloves when handling cooked beetroot if you want to avoid stained hands, the pigment is extremely persistent on skin and clothing.

items.prepNote: medium, scrubbed, unpeeled, stems trimmed to 2 cm

content.text: Add 300 ml of water to the pressure cooker and place the trivet inside. Arrange the whole scrubbed beetroot on the trivet, do not peel or cut them. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes for medium beetroot (about 6 to 7 cm diameter), or 25 minutes for larger ones. Quick-release the pressure.

Test the beetroot with a skewer, it should slide in with no resistance. Transfer to a bowl of cold water and leave for 5 minutes. Wearing rubber gloves, rub the skins off, they will slip away easily. The beetroot is now ready to slice, dice, or leave whole.

rows.symptom: The beetroot is still firm in the centre
rows.cause: The beetroot was larger than medium, or the pressure cooker did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 10 minutes. Very large beetroot can take up to 35 minutes.

rows.symptom: The skin is difficult to remove
rows.cause: The beetroot needs more time in cold water to loosen the skin.
rows.fix: Leave in cold water for a further 5 minutes. The skin should then rub off easily.

rows.symptom: The beetroot has a muted colour
rows.cause: The skin was breached before cooking, allowing pigment to leach out.
rows.fix: Cook whole and unpeeled with the stem trimmed to 2 cm, not flush. Breaking the skin seal allows the pigment to escape into the water.

content.text: Cooked beetroot is a building block rather than a finished dish. Slice into salads with goat's cheese and walnuts, dice into grain bowls, blend into hummus or a borscht-style soup, or serve warm alongside roasted meats. The pressure cooker makes a batch practical, cook four or six at once and use them across the week, stored in the fridge in their skins or peeled and covered with a little vinegar.
